claim: HABITS enables free-moving mice to learn challenging cognitive behaviors in their home-cage without any human involvement.

claim: Mice actually needed more water throughout the day than provided in manual training.
source: At the end of manual training, we transferred all mice to autonomous testing and found that the number of trial and consumption water per day dramatically increased to the level of the autonomous training, suggesting mice actually needed more water throughout the day (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Autonomous training achieved similar training performance as manual training and maintained a more healthy state of mice.
source: These results indicated that autonomous training achieved similar training performance as manual training and maintained a more healthy state of mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparative data presented.

claim: 10 mice were trained on sound orientation d2AFC task.
source: Three more cohorts of mice were used in d2AFC tasks with different modalities, which included sound orientation (left vs. right sound), light orientation (left vs. right light), and light color (red vs. blue). Using the same training protocol as in the sound frequency modality, we trained 10, 11, and 8 mice on these tasks, respectively (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2I.

claim: 11 mice were trained on light orientation d2AFC task.
source: Three more cohorts of mice were used in d2AFC tasks with different modalities, which included sound orientation (left vs. right sound), light orientation (left vs. right light), and light color (red vs. blue). Using the same training protocol as in the sound frequency modality, we trained 10, 11, and 8 mice on these tasks, respectively (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2I.

claim: 8 mice were trained on light color d2AFC task.
source: Three more cohorts of mice were used in d2AFC tasks with different modalities, which included sound orientation (left vs. right sound), light orientation (left vs. right light), and light color (red vs. blue). Using the same training protocol as in the sound frequency modality, we trained 10, 11, and 8 mice on these tasks, respectively (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Light color discrimination was the most challenging modality, requiring an average of 82,932±6817 trials.
source: Mice required different amounts of trials or days to discriminate these modalities, with light color discrimination being the most challenging (an average of 82,932±6817 trials), consistent with the limited sensitivity to light wavelength of mice (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The difficulty of light color discrimination is consistent with the limited sensitivity to light wavelength of mice.
source: Mice required different amounts of trials or days to discriminate these modalities, with light color discrimination being the most challenging (an average of 82,932±6817 trials), consistent with the limited sensitivity to light wavelength of mice (Figure 2J).
evidence: This connects the experimental observation to known mouse physiology.

claim: The learning rate between sound and light orientation discrimination tasks was similar (p=0.439).
source: The learning rate between sound and light orientation discrimination tasks was similar (p=0.439, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test), but the variation for light orientation was large, indicating possible individual differences (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The variation for light orientation learning was large, indicating possible individual differences.
source: The learning rate between sound and light orientation discrimination tasks was similar (p=0.439, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test), but the variation for light orientation was large, indicating possible individual differences (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is an inference from the data variability shown in Figure 2J.

claim: All modalities maintained good health state indicated by body weight for up to 2 months.
source: All modalities maintained good health state indicated by the body weight for up to 2 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: RT-2AFC task was successfully tested in HABITS.
source: Another two types of 2AFC, reaction time (Munoz and Everling, 2004) (RT-2AFC, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and random foraging (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) task, were also successfully tested in HABITS.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Random foraging task was successfully tested in HABITS.
source: Another two types of 2AFC, reaction time (Munoz and Everling, 2004) (RT-2AFC, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and random foraging (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) task, were also successfully tested in HABITS.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The dynamic foraging task was first demonstrated in a fully autonomous training scheme for freely moving mice.
source: Notably, the dynamic foraging task (Hattori et al., 2023; Hattori et al., 2019), which heavily relies on historical information, was first demonstrated in a fully autonomous training scheme for freely moving mice with similar block size and performance.
evidence: This is a claim of novelty supported by citations to previous work on this task.

claim: All mice exhibited clear nocturnal behavior with peaks in trial proportion at the beginning and end of the dark period.
source: We found all mice exhibited clear nocturnal behavior with peaks in trial proportion at the beginning and end of the dark period (Figure 2K), which was consistent with previous studies (Francis et al., 2019; Hao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2K and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The light color modality exhibited a slightly lower percentage of trials during dark (57.89%±3.18% vs. above 66% for other modalities).
source: The light color modality exhibited a slightly lower percentage of trials during dark (57.89% ± 3.18% vs. above 66% for other modalities; Figure 2K), possibly the light stimulus during trials affected the circadian rhythms of the mice.
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Light stimulus during trials possibly affected the circadian rhythms of mice in the light color modality.
source: The light color modality exhibited a slightly lower percentage of trials during dark (57.89% ± 3.18% vs. above 66% for other modalities; Figure 2K), possibly the light stimulus during trials affected the circadian rhythms of the mice.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: All mice except the light color modality showed no significant differences in correct rate between light and dark cycle after learning.
source: It was also observed that all mice except the light color modality showed no significant differences in correct rate between light and dark cycle after they learned the task (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Light color modality showed higher performance in dark environment, implying light stimulus in dark has higher contrast and better discernibility.
source: The higher performance in a dark environment for light color modality implied that light stimulus presented in a dark environment was with higher contrast and thus better discernibility.
evidence: This is an inference from the performance difference observed.

claim: More than two-thirds of the trials were done in >5-trial blocks.
source: We found more than two-thirds of the trials were done in >5-trial blocks (Figure 2L left), which resulted in more than 55% of the trials being with inter-trial intervals less than 2 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2L left panel.

claim: More than 55% of the trials had inter-trial intervals less than 2 s.
source: We found more than two-thirds of the trials were done in >5-trial blocks (Figure 2L left), which resulted in more than 55% of the trials being with inter-trial intervals less than 2 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The averaged block duration was 27.64±1.73 s.
source: The averaged block duration was 27.64±1.73 s and mice triggered another block of trials within 60 s in more than 60% of cases.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: Mice triggered another block of trials within 60 s in more than 60% of cases.
source: The averaged block duration was 27.64±1.73 s and mice triggered another block of trials within 60 s in more than 60% of cases.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: The averaged correct rate increased as the length of the block increased.
source: Meanwhile, we also found that the averaged correct rate increased and the early lick rate decreased as the length of the block increased (Figure 2L right), which suggested that mice were more engaged in the task during longer blocks.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2L right panel.

claim: The early lick rate decreased as the length of the block increased.
source: Meanwhile, we also found that the averaged correct rate increased and the early lick rate decreased as the length of the block increased (Figure 2L right), which suggested that mice were more engaged in the task during longer blocks.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2L right panel.

claim: Mice were more engaged in the task during longer blocks.
source: Meanwhile, we also found that the averaged correct rate increased and the early lick rate decreased as the length of the block increased (Figure 2L right), which suggested that mice were more engaged in the task during longer blocks.
evidence: This is an inference from the performance patterns shown in Figure 2L.

claim: All mice (8/8) underwent contingency reversal for an average of 52.25±16.39 times.
source: Given the advantages of long-term autonomous training in HABITS, all mice underwent contingency reversal for an average of 52.25±16.39 times, and one mouse achieved up to 125 times in 113 days.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the contingency reversal experiments.

claim: One mouse achieved up to 125 contingency reversals in 113 days.
source: Given the advantages of long-term autonomous training in HABITS, all mice underwent contingency reversal for an average of 52.25±16.39 times, and one mouse achieved up to 125 times in 113 days.
evidence: This is a specific data point highlighting the capability for long-term training.

claim: Most mice (6/8) gradually decreased the number of trials to reach criterion across multiple contingency reversals, representing learning to learn.
source: Most of the mice (6/8) gradually decreased the number of trials to reach criterion across multiple contingency reversals representing an effect of learning to learn (Hattori et al., 2023; Akrami et al., 2018; Figure 3A3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A3 and supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The average number of trials to reach criterion during reversal was highly correlated with the trial number in the first reversal learning.
source: Meanwhile, the average number of trials to reach criterion during the reversal was highly correlated with the trial number in the first reversal learning which represented the initial cognitive ability or the sensory sensitivity of individual mice (Figure 3A4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A4.

claim: 8/10 mice were successfully trained in the evidence accumulation task.
source: We successfully trained 8/10 mice to complete this task as revealed by the psychometric curves (Figure 3C2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C2.

claim: All mice in evidence accumulation task exhibited behavioral patterns correlated with evidence of stimulus.
source: All mice exhibited consistent behavioral patterns, which were correlated with the evidence of stimulus, that is longer sample period and/or higher stimulus contrast led to higher performance (Figure 3C3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C3.

claim: Longer sample period led to higher performance in evidence accumulation task.
source: All mice exhibited consistent behavioral patterns, which were correlated with the evidence of stimulus, that is longer sample period and/or higher stimulus contrast led to higher performance (Figure 3C3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C3.

claim: Higher stimulus contrast led to higher performance in evidence accumulation task.
source: All mice exhibited consistent behavioral patterns, which were correlated with the evidence of stimulus, that is longer sample period and/or higher stimulus contrast led to higher performance (Figure 3C3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C3.

claim: 13/15 mice were successfully trained in multimodal integration paradigm with multimodal or sound clicks stimulus.
source: We successfully trained 13/15 mice in this paradigm with multimodal or sound clicks stimulus (Figure 3D2), and only three mice achieved performance criteria in trials with light flashes stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D2.

claim: Only three mice achieved performance criteria in trials with light flashes stimulus in multimodal integration task.
source: We successfully trained 13/15 mice in this paradigm with multimodal or sound clicks stimulus (Figure 3D2), and only three mice achieved performance criteria in trials with light flashes stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D2.

claim: Mice tended to favor earlier stimuli in making their final choices in multimodal integration task.
source: We found that mice indeed tended to favor earlier stimuli (i.e. higher weights) in making their final choices (Figure 3D4), consistent with previous research findings (Odoemene et al., 2018).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D4 and supported by citation to previous research.

claim: 5/6 mice were successfully trained in the confidence-probing task.
source: We successfully trained 5/6 mice (Figure 3E2), and most importantly, there was a noticeable difference of TI in correct versus incorrect trials (Figure 3E3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E2.

claim: There was a noticeable difference of time investment (TI) in correct versus incorrect trials in confidence-probing task.
source: We successfully trained 5/6 mice (Figure 3E2), and most importantly, there was a noticeable difference of TI in correct versus incorrect trials (Figure 3E3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E3.

claim: Trials with longer TIs tended to have higher accuracies in confidence-probing task.
source: In detail, trials with longer TIs tended to have higher accuracies (Figure 3E4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E4.

claim: As contrast decreased, mice exhibited reduced confidence about their choices in confidence-probing task.
source: Furthermore, the TI was also modulated by the contrasts of stimuli; as contrast decreased, mice exhibited reduced confidence about their choices, manifesting as decreased willingness to wait in correct trials, and conversely in error trials (Figure 3E5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E5.

claim: Mice could quickly switch from one task to another in continuous learning, with learning rates following the difficulty of modalities.
source: Firstly, the results showed that mice could quickly switch from one task to another and the learning rates across these sub-tasks roughly followed the learning difficulty of modalities (Figure 4A2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A2.

claim: Reversal of sound frequency was cognitively different from reversal of sound orientation, resulting in significantly longer learning duration.
source: Specifically, reversal of sound frequency was cognitively different from reversal of sound orientation (i.e., from pro to anti), which resulted in significantly longer learning duration (Figure 4A2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A2.

claim: Mice dealt with new tasks with higher reaction time and gradually decreased as training progressed in continuous learning.
source: Secondly, mice dealt with new tasks with higher reaction time and gradually decreased as training progressed (Figure 4A3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A3.

claim: Mice chose to respond more slowly in order to learn quickly in continuous learning.
source: It implied a uniform strategy mice applied: mice chose to respond more slowly in order to learn quickly (Masís et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference from the reaction time data, supported by citation.

claim: Mice exhibited large bias at the beginning of each task in continuous learning, including tasks without reversals.
source: Lastly, mice exhibited large bias at the beginning of each task in all tasks, including tasks without reversals (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mice acquired reward only from one lickport in early training and switched strategy to follow current stimulus gradually.
source: This means that mice acquired reward only from one lickport in the early training and switched strategy to follow current stimulus gradually, which implied a changing strategy from exploration to exploitation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the bias data.

claim: All 10 mice achieved performance criteria in dDMS task during automated training.
source: All the 10 mice achieved the performance criteria during the automated training process, though, an averaged 64.45±7.88 days was required, which was equivalent to more than 120,000 trials (Figure 4B2-3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B2-3.

claim: dDMS task required an average of 64.45±7.88 days, equivalent to more than 120,000 trials.
source: All the 10 mice achieved the performance criteria during the automated training process, though, an averaged 64.45±7.88 days was required, which was equivalent to more than 120,000 trials (Figure 4B2-3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the training data.

claim: The four trial types in dDMS achieved equally well performance after training.
source: After training, the four trial types (i.e. four combinations of frequencies) achieved equally well performance (Figure 4B4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B4.

claim: Error rates and early lick rates increased as delay duration increased in dDMS task.
source: During the testing stage, we systematically randomized the duration of the two delays (ranging from 1 to 3 s) and revealed increased error rates and early lick rates as the delay increased (Figure 4B5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B5.

claim: All 14 mice were successfully trained in d3AFC task in 13.85±1.05 days.
source: We successfully trained all the 14 mice to perform the tasks in 13.85±1.05 days, with similar performance among the left, middle, and right trial types (Figure 4C2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C2.

claim: The final correct rate and early lick rate made no differences for the three trial types in d3AFC.
source: The final correct rate and early lick rate made no differences for the three trial types (Figure 4C3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C3.

claim: Mice made error choices more in the most proximity lickport in d3AFC.
source: Interestingly, mice made error choices more in the most proximity lickport; for the middle trials, mice made error choices equally in the left and right sides (Figure 4C4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C4.

claim: Mice presented two evident psychological thresholds to deal with d3AFC task.
source: In addition, we tested the whole spectrum of sound frequencies between 8 and 32 kHz and found that mice presented two evident psychological thresholds to deal with this three-choice task (Figure 4C5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C5.

claim: Sound orientation-based d3AFC required longer training duration (45.16±11.46 days) than frequency-based d3AFC.
source: Finally, we also implemented sound orientation-based d3AFC in another separated group of mice, which actually required longer training duration (45.16±11.46 days) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All six mice were successfully trained in context-dependent attention task with an average of 48.09±7.54 days.
source: We successfully trained all six mice enrolled in this task, with an average of 48.09±7.54 days (Figure 4D2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D2.

claim: Mice exceeded criterion performance across different trial types in context-dependent attention task.
source: Mice exceeded criterion performance across different trial types (i.e. unimodal, multimodal w/ conflict, multimodal w/o conflict), indicating effective attention to both stimulus features (Figure 4D3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D3.

claim: Trials with conflicting stimulus features exhibited reduced decision speeds and accuracy compared to trials without conflicting in context-dependent attention task.
source: Trials with conflicting stimulus features, requiring mice to integrate context information for correct choice, exhibited reduced decision speeds and accuracy compared to trials without conflicting for all tested mice (Figure 4D3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D3.

claim: For trials with conflicts, mice decreased accuracy following decline of context contrast in context-dependent attention task.
source: For trials with conflicts, mice decreased their accuracy following the decline of context contrast, formulating a flat psychometric curve. However, for trials without conflicts, mice performed as a near-optimal learner (Figure 4D4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D4.

claim: For trials without conflicts, mice performed as a near-optimal learner in context-dependent attention task.
source: For trials with conflicts, mice decreased their accuracy following the decline of context contrast, formulating a flat psychometric curve. However, for trials without conflicts, mice performed as a near-optimal learner (Figure 4D4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D4.

claim: As context contrast decreased, mice tended to bias to orientation feature against frequency in conflicting trials.
source: Meanwhile, as the contrast decreased, mice tended to bias to orientation feature against frequency in conflicting trials, but not for the trials without conflicts (Figure 4D5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D5.

claim: Performance of both trial types declined with increased delay duration but maintained criterion above up to 2 s delay in context-dependent attention task.
source: Lastly, the performance of both trial types declined with increased delay duration but maintained criterion above up to 2 s delay (Figure 4D6), confirming mice could execute this paradigm robustly in our system.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D6.

claim: Mice trained with MT algorithm achieved criteria performance with significantly fewer trials compared with random group in working memory task.
source: Mice trained with the MT algorithm achieved criteria performance with significantly fewer trials compared with the random group (Figure 5C); three out of the eight mice in the random group even did not reach the criteria performance at the end of training (60 days).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Three out of eight mice in the random group did not reach criteria performance at the end of training (60 days) in working memory task.
source: Mice trained with the MT algorithm achieved criteria performance with significantly fewer trials compared with the random group (Figure 5C); three out of the eight mice in the random group even did not reach the criteria performance at the end of training (60 days).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MT-based training presented easier trials first, then gradually increased difficulty, exhibiting curriculum learning trajectory.
source: Analysis of the trial type across learning revealed that the MT-based training presented easier trials first, then gradually increased the difficulty, that is exhibiting a clear curriculum learning trajectory (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: MT strategy enabled mice to maintain consistently higher performance than random groups throughout training in working memory task.
source: This strategy enabled mice to maintain consistently higher performance than random groups throughout the training process (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: All three groups of mice achieved successful training in 2AFC task with comparable efficiency and final performance.
source: Due to the fact that this task was relatively simple, all three groups of mice achieved successful training, with comparable efficiency and final performance (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F.

claim: MT algorithm effectively reduced mice's preference towards a specific lickport (bias) throughout training in 2AFC task.
source: But interestingly, the MT algorithm effectively reduced mice's preference towards a specific lickport (i.e. bias; Figure 5G) throughout the training process by generating trial types with opposite bias more aggressively (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G and 5H.

claim: MT algorithm minimized bias dependency without increasing mice's reliance on other noise variables in 2AFC task.
source: Using a model-based methodology, we demonstrated that while the MT algorithm minimized bias dependency, it did not increase, and even decreased, mice's reliance on other noise variables, like previous action A1, reward R1 and stimulus S1 (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I.

claim: MT group had significantly higher weights for S0 than both anti-bias and random groups in trained stages of 2AFC task.
source: However, when we examined the reliance on the current stimulus S0, that is to what extent the decision was made according to current stimulus, we found that the MT group had significantly higher weights for S0 than both anti-bias and random groups (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5K.

claim: MT-generated sequences encouraged mice to rely only on current stimuli rather than noise factors across all stages.
source: This means that MT-generated sequences across all stages encouraged mice to rely only on current stimuli, rather than noise factors.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results shown in Figure 5K.

claim: MT algorithm manifested higher quality training results in both training and trained stages.
source: These results suggested that MT-based training had higher quality for both training and trained stage.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Both groups of mice successfully completed all goals in multi-dimensional task, achieving overall correct rate over 80%.
source: Both groups of mice successfully completed all the goals, achieving an overall correct rate of over 80% (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: MT group exhibited significantly higher learning rate compared to random group in the second goal of multi-dimensional task training.
source: During the first and the third goal of training, the learning rates of mice in both groups were similar, showing low sensitivity to irrelevant cue. However, in the second goal of training (i.e. transition from orientation to frequency modality), the MT group exhibited a significantly higher learning rate compared to the random group, along with a significantly faster rate of forgetting of the irrelevant cue (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: MT group showed significantly faster rate of forgetting of the irrelevant cue in the second goal of multi-dimensional task training.
source: During the first and the third goal of training, the learning rates of mice in both groups were similar, showing low sensitivity to irrelevant cue. However, in the second goal of training (i.e. transition from orientation to frequency modality), the MT group exhibited a significantly higher learning rate compared to the random group, along with a significantly faster rate of forgetting of the irrelevant cue (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: MT algorithm quickly suppressed sensitivity of irrelevant modality while keeping low sensitivity to noise dimensions in multi-dimensional task.
source: MT algorithm manifested distinct learning path against random group in the space (Figure 6E); MT algorithm quickly suppressed the sensitivity of irrelevant modality (i.e. Worient.), keeping low sensitivity to noise dimensions (i.e. Wnoise) in the meantime.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E.

claim: MT algorithm resulted in a circuitous learning path in latent space compared to random group in multi-dimensional task.
source: This resulted in a circuitous learning path in the space compared to the random group.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 6E.

claim: MT algorithm effectively suppressed mice's reliance on irrelevant strategies by dynamically adjusting ratio of stay/switch trials and left/right trial types.
source: Compared to the random sequence, the MT algorithm effectively suppressed the mice's reliance on irrelevant strategies by dynamically adjusting the ratio of stay/switch trials and left/right trial types (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mice trained with MT algorithm exhibited significantly lower left/right bias and stay/switch bias compared to randomly trained mice in testing.
source: Notably, those mice trained with the MT algorithm exhibited significantly lower left/right bias and stay/switch bias compared to the randomly trained mice (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: MT algorithm enabled mice to exhibit more stable and task-aligned behavioral training.
source: This suggested that the MT algorithm enabled mice to exhibit more stable and task-aligned behavioral training, which implied an internal influence to psychological decision strategies after the MT conditioning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results shown in Figure 6G.

claim: This study presents an extensive behavioral dataset derived from ~300 mice training and testing in more than 20 diverse paradigms.
source: One of the pivotal contributions of this research is the provision of an extensive behavioral dataset, derived from ~300 mice training and testing in more than 20 diverse paradigms.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Table 1.

claim: The comprehensive dataset consisted of the entire learning trajectory with well-documented training strategies and behavioral outcomes.
source: This comprehensive dataset consisted of the entire learning trajectory with well-documented training strategies and behavioral outcomes.
evidence: This describes the nature of the data collected.

claim: This is the first study demonstrating the utility of machine teaching in augmenting animal behavioral training.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first study demonstrating the utility of machine teaching in augmenting animal behavioral training, which complements previous simulation studies Bak et al., 2016.
evidence: This is a claim of novelty supported by citation to previous simulation work.

claim: Machine teaching reduced training duration of complex tasks primarily by real-time optimization of trial sequences based on mouse performance.
source: First, the training duration of complex tasks was substantially reduced, primarily due to the real-time optimization of trial sequences based on mouse performance, which significantly reduces the mice's reliance on suboptimal strategies.
evidence: This is a summary of the MT algorithm's effects based on the experimental results.

claim: Final training outcomes with MT were less influenced by task-irrelevant variables.
source: Second, the final training outcomes were demonstrated to be less influenced by the task-irrelevant variables.
evidence: This is based on the results shown in Figure 5 and Figure 6.

claim: Suboptimal strategies like biases are common among expert mice trained in various paradigms.
source: A prior study has indicated that suboptimal strategies, such as biases, are common among expert mice trained in various paradigms, potentially stemming from their exploration in real-world uncertain environments (Pisupati et al., 2021; Rosenberg et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023; Zhu and Kuchibhotla, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Machine teaching-based techniques can significantly reduce noise dependency in behavioral training.
source: Machine teaching-based techniques can significantly reduce the noise dependency, thus facilitating the analysis of the relationship between behavior and neural signals.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results and their implications.

claim: The machine learning algorithm lowers barriers for designing effective anti-bias strategies in multidimensional tasks.
source: Third, the machine learning algorithm lowers the barriers for designing effective anti-bias strategies, which were challenging and prone to lopsided in multidimensional tasks.
evidence: This is based on the demonstration of MT in multi-dimensional tasks.

claim: By setting task goals in the fitted decision model, machine teaching can automatically guide the mouse to approach the goal optimally and robustly.
source: By simply setting the task goals in the fitted decision model, machine teaching can automatically guide the mouse to approach the goal optimally and robustly.
evidence: This describes a capability of the MT algorithm demonstrated in the experiments.
